newsitem.title: FINLAND: ICE HOCKEY-FAVOURITES WIN FIRST DAY MATCHES.
newsitem.headline: ICE HOCKEY-FAVOURITES WIN FIRST DAY MATCHES.

text.p: The favourites lived up to expectations and beat lower-ranked opponents as the ice hockey world championship began on Saturday.
The Czech defending champions, Olympic champions Sweden, home favourites Finland -- the 1995 world champions -- and Canada, world champions in 1994, all won.
The results indicate that speculation of a clear divide between six stronger and six weaker teams may be proved right.
This casts doubt over the international ice hockey federation's (IIHF) decision to expand the 1998 championship from 12 teams to 16.

Even ardent supporters may find it hard to be thrilled if victory margins grow beyond Canada's 7-0 thrashing of Norway in group B in Turku, or Finland's 6-1 triumph over France in group A in Helsinki.
Also playing in Turku, Sweden beat Italy 5-3 while in Helsinki, the Czechs came from behind to edge Germany 2-1.
Geoff Sanderson scored twice while Sean Burke and Rick Tabaracci shared in the shutout for Canada over Norway.

Bob Errey and Sanderson broke open the contest midway through the first period and Owen Nolan, Keith Primeau, Anson Carter and Rob Zamuner all scored in the second as Canada recorded their biggest world championship win since beating Austria 11-0 in 1993.
"We were worried about playing Norway," said Canadian coach Andy Murray. "The first game of any tournament is difficult, playing an opponent you know nothing about."
Finnish coach Curt Lindstrom said his team had been anxious to conserve their strength ahead of "our tough game tomorrow against the Czechs."
"I am very happy to have started the tournament with a victory. The team did very well," Lindstrom said.
The game offered the Finnish side little more than a light warm-up.
Cheered by over 13,000 fans, among them President Martti Ahtisaari, who formally opened the championships, the Finns scored after barely two minutes and never looked back.
Kai Nurminen and Olli Jokinen had two goals each to the delight of the flag-waving capacity crowd in the brand new Hartwall Arena.
Vladimir Vujtek set up two goals in the last 15 minutes to save the day for the Czechs, who had failed to outsmart German goalkeeper Joseph Heiss in the first two periods of their opening match.
In the third period, the Czechs strung together the kind of passes that had eluded them in the opening 40 minutes, though they were still but a shadow of the side who won gold in Vienna last year.
"We knew it would be difficult to play Germany, but it became even more diffcult than we had expected," Czech coach Slavomir Lener said.
Jorgen Jonsson scored twice, including the clinching third period goal to give Sweden a 5-3 win over Italy.
Sweden appeared to take control midway through the second period when Michael Nylander and Niklas Sundblad scored 64 seconds apart to make it 4-2.
But Gaetano Orlando knocked in a loose puck from a goalmouth scramble to notch his second of the period and cut the deficit to one.

On Sunday, the first round of games in the round-robin groups will be completed as Russia play Slovakia in Helsinki and the United States face Latvia in Turku. If the pundits are right, Russia and the U.S. will sail to easy wins.
The first indication of the relative strengths of the top teams will be provided by Sunday's group A clash between Finland and the Czech Republic, and in group B between Sweden and Canada.
The top three teams from each group advance to the final series.
